Apex InsightOctober 3, 2026

The Brake Is Biting in the Wrong Places

Higher rates are suppressing labor mobility, wage growth, and market participation while energy and industrial supply constraints keep inflation elevated. The mismatch is widening the gap between headline strength and the pressure underneath.

Key Conclusions

  • Treasury volatility has surged without a comparable rise in index volatility because the rates shock is still being absorbed through rotation, dispersion, and weaker breadth rather than systemic selling.
  • Roughly one-quarter of S&P 500 constituents now exhibit a negative 63-day beta, making the headline index a less representative description of its own underlying market.
  • Labor remains low-hire and low-fire, but falling quits and a near-zero labor differential show that worker mobility, bargaining power, and wage growth are deteriorating.
  • Inflation pressure is increasingly concentrated in energy and industrial bottlenecks that monetary policy cannot directly repair, sharpening the tradeoff between price stability and employment.
Opening Argument

The Brake Is Biting in the Wrong Places

The macro environment is becoming increasingly defined by a divergence between where the pressure is building and where it is ultimately being absorbed. The rates market is already trading considerable uncertainty, yet the S&P 500 remains close to its highs. Inflation pressure is rebuilding across parts of the physical economy, yet the labor market is losing momentum and wage growth continues slowing. The result is an economy and market that remain resilient at the aggregate level while becoming considerably more fragmented underneath.

That fragmentation matters because the Fed's two mandates are beginning to pull policy in opposite directions. Supply constraints, elevated energy prices, and a still-expanding manufacturing cycle argue against declaring victory on inflation. At the same time, weaker payroll growth, declining worker mobility, and slowing wages suggest monetary restraint is already working through the parts of the economy it can most directly influence. Markets are experiencing the same divide as higher rates pressure broad participation while concentrated Technology leadership continues insulating the headline index.

The question from here is increasingly about transmission. Higher rates have clearly affected duration, rate-sensitive equities, labor mobility, and market breadth. What they have not yet produced is a broad firing cycle, material credit stress, or synchronized equity volatility. How long that separation can persist is becoming the central issue for both policy and markets.

Rates Volatility

Treasury Stress Has Not Become Index Stress

Interest-rate volatility remains at the center of the current market structure, even though the headline S&P 500 continues to make the environment look considerably calmer than it is underneath the surface. The index has largely consolidated sideways near its highs, but leadership remains narrow and the average stock has experienced substantially more pressure. Elevated long-term rates are increasingly visible across the rate-sensitive portions of the equity market. Small Caps, Cyclicals, Defensives, and the equal-weighted S&P 500 have all weakened while a relatively small group of mega-cap Technology companies continues doing much of the work required to hold the capitalization-weighted index together.

The Treasury market is where that pressure remains most obvious. The 10-year yield has pushed toward 5.30%, approaching levels last seen in 2007, while TLT has moved to new lows. The rates market has also repriced the Fed substantially, with investors assigning elevated probabilities to additional tightening at the remaining 2026 meetings and multiple hikes now embedded over the coming year. The combination has produced one of the largest and fastest increases in yields of the current cycle, leaving duration extended both relative to its recent trend and the post-GFC range investors had become accustomed to.

There is no single explanation for the move. Strong nominal growth continues to reduce the urgency for investors to own duration. Oil remains elevated and has maintained a strong relationship with Treasury yields as the Iran conflict keeps inflation uncertainty alive. Fiscal deficits and enormous financing requirements continue adding pressure through term premium, while the Fed's September hike and more hawkish projected policy path forced another repricing of the expected short-rate component. The long end is therefore absorbing pressure from growth, inflation, monetary policy, commodity prices, and fiscal risk simultaneously.

The important point is that stretched conditions are not themselves a catalyst for reversal. Treasury positioning remains extreme, yields have moved unusually far and fast, and duration is increasingly oversold, but markets can remain extended when the fundamental forces producing that extension remain intact. A meaningful reversal still requires something to change, whether through weaker growth, lower oil, softer inflation, a change in the Fed's reaction function, or evidence that higher rates are beginning to damage the economy sufficiently to create demand for duration.

The chart below shows why the current environment is particularly interesting. The spread between the MOVE Index and the VIX has surged to roughly 92 points, with MOVE around 107 while the VIX remains near 15. The Treasury market is pricing a substantially larger degree of uncertainty than the equity index. The spread has returned toward levels last seen during periods of considerably greater concern in the rates market, yet that volatility has still not migrated into headline equity volatility.

That divergence tells us something important. The market is not broadly calm. The calm is concentrated in the index. Treasury investors are dealing with substantial uncertainty around inflation, Fed policy, fiscal supply, and the clearing price for duration. Individual equities are also experiencing elevated volatility, as reflected in VIXEQ, while dispersion remains high. What has remained suppressed is the volatility of the S&P 500 as a portfolio because those individual stock moves continue offsetting one another rather than becoming highly correlated.

This is consistent with the breadth deterioration discussed in our previous note. The capitalization-weighted index can remain close to its highs while substantial portions of the market correct underneath it because weakness in Small Caps, rate-sensitive sectors, Defensives, and the average S&P 500 constituent is being offset by strength in the largest Technology companies. High dispersion allows that process to continue without producing the type of synchronized selling that normally sends the VIX sharply higher.

In some ways, this makes the MOVE-VIX divergence more informative than either index in isolation. MOVE is telling us that uncertainty around the discount rate has increased substantially. VIX is telling us that investors still do not expect that uncertainty to translate into a large near-term move in the S&P 500. Both can remain true as long as corporate earnings remain strong, credit remains orderly, and mega-cap leadership continues offsetting weakness elsewhere.

The transmission channel we continue to watch is credit. Credit Spreads have begun to move modestly, but they have not widened enough to suggest that the rates shock has developed into a broader funding problem. That distinction remains critical. Higher Treasury yields with contained Credit Spreads represent a valuation and cost-of-capital problem. Higher Treasury yields accompanied by a sustained widening in Credit Spreads would tell us that the pressure is migrating from the risk-free curve into corporate financing conditions and the underlying economy.

The same logic applies to equity volatility. The VIX does not need to rise simply because MOVE is elevated. But the combination of high single-stock volatility and high dispersion creates a market that is more dependent on low correlation remaining intact. If the macro catalyst changes and correlations begin rising, the individual volatility that is currently cancelling out inside the index can begin reinforcing itself instead. That is the mechanism through which a seemingly calm S&P 500 can transition relatively quickly into higher index volatility.

For now, that transition has not occurred. The S&P 500 remains resilient, the VIX remains subdued, and credit has not confirmed systemic stress. The market is absorbing a historically significant rates repricing primarily through rotation, breadth deterioration, and pressure on rate-sensitive assets rather than through indiscriminate liquidation.

That makes the current divergence less a prediction of an imminent equity correction than a measure of where the stress currently resides. The bond market is already trading the uncertainty. The average stock is increasingly feeling the consequences. The S&P 500 itself has not yet been forced to acknowledge either one.

The next important signal is whether that separation persists. If yields stabilize or reverse, the substantial pressure already absorbed beneath the index could provide the foundation for a powerful breadth recovery. If rates continue higher and MOVE remains elevated, the more consequential test becomes whether credit, correlation, and ultimately the VIX begin catching up.

Market Structure

The Index Is No Longer Describing Its Constituents

What is particularly interesting in the current market structure is the unusually large share of S&P 500 constituents now exhibiting a negative beta to the index. Using the 503 constituents in the chart below, roughly 27% currently have a negative 63-day beta, down from a recent peak above 40% but still extraordinarily elevated relative to the past several years. In simple terms, more than one-quarter of the index has recently tended to move in the opposite direction of the S&P 500 itself.

That is a very different signal from conventional breadth. A stock does not need to be falling to have negative beta. Negative beta means its returns have exhibited negative covariance with the index over the measurement window. When the S&P 500 rises, these stocks have tended to lag or move lower, and when the index falls, they have tended to hold up or move in the opposite direction. When that behavior expands across a large portion of the index, it tells us the market is becoming increasingly internally divided.

That fits the broader structure we have been documenting. A relatively narrow group of large Technology companies continues to determine the direction of the capitalization-weighted index, while substantial portions of the remaining market respond very differently to rates, commodities, sector-specific fundamentals, and other macro forces. The S&P 500 can therefore remain near its highs even as an unusually large share of its own constituents develops a negative relationship with the index they comprise.

Historically, spikes in negative-beta breadth have often occurred around larger market drawdowns, but the mechanism is more important than treating the indicator as a timing signal. During periods of significant internal dislocation, the market effectively stops behaving like one market. Leadership becomes concentrated, cross-sectional differences widen, and the relationship between the index and its constituents becomes increasingly unstable. Large index declines can subsequently restore a more conventional correlation structure as macro risk overwhelms stock-specific and sector-specific differences and everything begins moving together again.

The current reading is therefore another indication that the calm visible in SPY is masking an unusually fragmented market underneath. It does not tell us that an index correction must occur, particularly while mega-cap leadership remains strong. But it does tell us that the S&P 500's current price is becoming a less representative description of what is happening to the stocks inside it.

The constructive resolution would be rotation. If rates stabilize and participation broadens, many of these negative-beta relationships can normalize as the rest of the market begins participating alongside Technology. The less constructive resolution occurs if the narrow group supporting the index finally weakens. In that environment, the internal offset that has kept SPY stable disappears and correlations can rise rapidly.

For now, the important message is not simply that breadth is weak. The market is increasingly behaving as two different markets at once. With roughly one-quarter of S&P 500 constituents exhibiting negative beta to the index, the divergence between headline index performance and the underlying constituent experience has become unusually large.

Labor Mobility

Job Security Is Holding While Outside Options Disappear

There was a large amount of macro data released this week, but very little changed the broader labor-market narrative. The JOLTS report continued to describe an economy where labor demand is cooling without transitioning into a firing cycle. Job Openings fell by 256K to 7.079 million in August, leaving roughly 1.01 openings per unemployed worker, dramatically below the 2.0 peak reached in 2022 and now much closer to pre-pandemic norms. The openings rate also slipped to 4.3%, reinforcing the broader evidence that businesses have become considerably less aggressive in competing for incremental workers.

The actual labor flows were somewhat more constructive. Hires increased by 46K to 5.192 million and the Hiring Rate ticked higher to 3.3% from 3.2%, while Layoffs and Discharges fell by 61K to 1.641 million, the lowest level in 17 months. The Layoff Rate remains only 1.0%. Quits were little changed near 3.1 million and the Quits Rate remained at 1.9%. That combination continues to fit the low-hire, low-fire framework we have discussed for much of this cycle. Companies are not aggressively expanding payrolls, but they are showing equally little interest in reducing existing headcount.

The JOLTS data should also be interpreted with some humility. Survey response rates remain substantially below their pre-pandemic levels, increasing the potential noise around individual monthly estimates and subsequent revisions. That makes the direction of the broader labor-flow data more useful when confirmed by Claims, payrolls, and business surveys than any single JOLTS print in isolation. Those other measures continue to support the same basic conclusion: layoffs remain exceptionally low while the ability to move between jobs has deteriorated considerably.

The Conference Board Consumer Confidence report shows what that environment feels like from the worker's perspective. Headline confidence fell sharply to 81.9 in September, the lowest level since April 2014, with both Current Conditions and Expectations deteriorating. More importantly for the labor discussion, the share of consumers describing jobs as "plentiful" declined to 23.6%, while those saying jobs were "hard to get" increased to 21.9%. The resulting Labor Differential collapsed to only +1.7 percentage points from +4.2, its weakest reading since early 2021.

The chart below ties that deterioration directly to the Quits Rate. Historically, these two measures have moved closely together because they capture different sides of the same decision. The Conference Board differential measures whether workers believe employment opportunities are readily available. The Quits Rate measures whether workers are confident enough in those opportunities to voluntarily leave their existing job. When jobs are plentiful, workers quit more frequently because the probability of finding a better position is high. When jobs become harder to find, workers stay put.

Both are now sending essentially the same message. The Quits Rate remains depressed at 1.9%, while the Labor Differential has fallen almost completely back toward zero. Workers increasingly perceive little advantage to testing the external labor market, and their actual behavior confirms it. This is not primarily a story about workers losing jobs. It is a story about the disappearance of outside options.

That distinction helps reconcile what otherwise looks contradictory in the labor data. Initial Claims remain near their lows, JOLTS layoffs just reached a 17-month low, and corporate profitability gives businesses little reason to aggressively reduce headcount. Yet unemployment duration is lengthening and consumers increasingly report that jobs are difficult to find. Both can be true when the inflow into unemployment remains low but the probability of exiting unemployment into a new job also declines.

This is why the current labor market can feel considerably weaker to households than the 4.2% Unemployment Rate suggests. Someone already employed still has relatively strong job security. Someone entering the workforce, attempting to change employers, or trying to find work after losing a position faces a very different market. The aggregate unemployment rate captures both groups imperfectly, while the Quits Rate and Labor Differential provide a clearer window into the collapse in worker optionality.

There is also an important implication for wages and inflation. A worker with fewer outside opportunities has considerably less bargaining power. Depressed quits reduce the need for employers to compete aggressively through compensation, which is one reason wage growth has continued moderating despite the absence of widespread layoffs. From that perspective, the deterioration shown below is another indication that the labor market itself is not the primary source of today's renewed inflation pressure.

The risk is what happens if the Fed continues tightening into this structure. Another hike does not need to immediately produce a surge in Claims to weaken employment conditions further. It can first reduce vacancies, suppress hiring, extend unemployment duration, and make workers even less willing to quit. The deterioration appears through mobility before it appears through layoffs.

For now, the distinction remains critical. Employers are still holding onto workers, but workers increasingly believe there is nowhere better to go. The Quits Rate and Labor Differential are telling the same story from opposite sides of the labor market: job security remains relatively strong for insiders, while opportunity continues deteriorating for everyone trying to move.

Inflation Source

The Bottleneck Is Industrial, Not Labor

The more persistent problem remains on the inflation side, where the current pressure increasingly looks like a collision between strong demand and constrained supply rather than a conventional wage-driven inflation cycle. Oil remains the most visible bottleneck following the Iran conflict, but the enormous buildout of data centers, power generation, transmission, semiconductors, electrical equipment, and related infrastructure is creating additional pressure across parts of the industrial supply chain. Those constraints matter because they can keep prices elevated even while the labor market itself continues cooling.

The chart below provides a useful way to see that pressure developing. We average the delivery-time diffusion indexes from the New York, Philadelphia, and Kansas City Fed manufacturing surveys and compare them with ISM Prices Paid. Rising delivery times indicate that manufacturers are waiting longer for inputs, generally because demand is outrunning available supply, transportation is constrained, or particular inputs have become difficult to source. Historically, those delays have maintained a close relationship with the prices manufacturers ultimately report paying.

That relationship has reemerged forcefully. The regional delivery-time average has climbed to roughly 21, while ISM Prices Paid surged to 77.9 in September from 71.1. ISM reported no commodities declining in price during the month. This is materially different from the disinflationary environment that followed the pandemic supply-chain normalization, when delivery times collapsed and goods-price pressure followed them lower. Today, the direction is reversing.

Importantly, this is occurring alongside a manufacturing economy that remains firmly expansionary. The September ISM Manufacturing PMI came in at 54.5, essentially unchanged from August's 54.6, marking the ninth consecutive month of expansion. ISM notes that a reading around this level has historically been consistent with approximately 2.4% annualized Real GDP growth. This is therefore not a case where prices are rising simply because supply is collapsing into a recessionary economy. Demand remains healthy enough to compete for constrained inputs.

The internals reinforce that interpretation. New Orders accelerated to 55.3 from 53.7 and Backlog of Orders jumped to 56.4 from 51.8, while Customer Inventories fell further to 41.6. Customers continue reporting inventories as too low at the same time new demand and backlogs are increasing. That combination creates pressure for future production because manufacturers need to satisfy current orders while customers eventually rebuild inventories.

Production remains strong at 56.7 despite moderating from 58.3, while Employment improved to 52.7 from 51.2, its third consecutive expansionary reading. That fits the broader labor picture discussed above. Aggregate hiring remains subdued, but selected cyclical and industrial areas continue adding workers as investment and manufacturing activity remain comparatively healthy.

The inflation problem is that this configuration does not naturally produce rapid goods disinflation. Strong New Orders, rising Backlogs, low Customer Inventories, longer Delivery Times, and elevated Prices Paid describe a supply chain operating with considerably less spare capacity than aggregate measures of the economy would imply. The bottlenecks are concentrated rather than universal, but they are concentrated in precisely the areas receiving enormous amounts of incremental capital.

That brings us back to the AI investment cycle. The longer-term productivity benefits can ultimately be disinflationary if companies produce more output with the same amount of labor and capital. The near-term buildout works differently. Data centers require power, transformers, turbines, cooling equipment, semiconductors, networking hardware, construction capacity, and specialized labor before those productivity benefits are fully realized. Demand for those inputs arrives immediately while new productive capacity can take years to build.

This is the difficult part of the Fed's current inflation problem. Higher policy rates cannot produce additional oil, shorten semiconductor lead times, manufacture transformers, or accelerate the construction of power generation and transmission infrastructure. Monetary policy can only reduce aggregate demand enough that buyers stop competing as aggressively for the constrained supply that exists.

That is a very blunt solution to a relatively concentrated problem. It means rate-sensitive portions of the economy such as housing, Small Caps, commercial real estate, and smaller businesses can absorb additional restraint even though they are not necessarily responsible for the supply bottlenecks keeping Prices Paid elevated.

The Fed's concern, however, is increasingly about allowing those bottlenecks to persist long enough that they migrate into broader inflation. Higher energy, transportation, electricity, and equipment costs eventually pressure margins. Businesses can then attempt to pass those costs through to customers, transforming a relative-price shock into a wider inflation process. After more than five years of above-target inflation, policymakers have become considerably less willing to assume that second-round effects will disappear without intervention.

For now, the labor data have reduced some of the urgency for immediate additional tightening. The combination of softer worker perceptions, depressed quits, and still-subdued hiring helped push an October hike farther out of the market's base case. December remains the more important meeting, with markets still assigning a high probability to another increase.

That leaves the Fed facing essentially the same asymmetry that has defined the past several months. The labor market is cooling in the places monetary policy can influence, while inflation pressure is persisting in several of the places monetary policy cannot directly fix.

The chart below captures that problem particularly well. Delivery times are lengthening and Prices Paid are rising while manufacturing demand remains expansionary. Until either supply catches up or demand slows enough to relieve those bottlenecks, the Fed's inflation problem is unlikely to disappear cleanly.

Wages and Income

Slower Wages Are Thinning the Consumer Cushion

The September employment report finally showed more meaningful weakness in the hiring side of the labor market, but it still did not produce the firing cycle that would indicate a conventional recessionary break. Nonfarm Payrolls increased only 29K versus roughly 90K expected, while July was revised into contraction and August was reduced to 133K. Combined revisions removed another 60K jobs from the prior two months, pulling the three-month average down to only 51K and the six-month average to 66K. The Private Employment Diffusion Index also fell below 50, indicating that slightly more industries are now reducing employment than expanding it.

The household survey was somewhat less concerning. The Unemployment Rate increased only modestly to 4.2%, while Labor Force Participation improved to 61.8% and the Employment-to-Population Ratio increased to 59.2%. U-6 Underemployment actually declined to 7.6%. Combined with Claims remaining near their lows and JOLTS layoffs falling to a 17-month low, the report continues to describe a labor market where the weakness is concentrated in job creation and mobility rather than job destruction.

That distinction connects directly with the Quits Rate and Labor Differential discussed above. Workers increasingly believe jobs are difficult to find, quits remain depressed at 1.9%, and businesses have become reluctant to add incremental headcount. September payrolls are increasingly confirming what those leading labor indicators have been signaling for some time. The labor market is not suddenly collapsing. It is gradually becoming less dynamic.

The chart below takes that framework one step further by connecting worker mobility directly to wages. Job Switchers continue to earn faster wage growth than Job Stayers, at roughly 4.4% versus 3.6%, but both have decelerated substantially from their post-pandemic peaks. Average Hourly Earnings provide confirmation from the establishment survey, slowing to only 0.1% month over month and 3.0% year over year.

The relationship makes intuitive sense. Workers generally receive the largest compensation increases when they can credibly leave one employer for another. During 2021 and 2022, extraordinarily high labor demand produced a surge in quits and employers were forced to compete aggressively for available workers. Wage growth for Job Switchers eventually approached 8%, pulling compensation higher across the broader labor market as companies also had to pay existing employees more to prevent them from leaving.

That mechanism is largely absent today. The wage premium for switching jobs still exists, but far fewer workers are exercising that option. With the Quits Rate at 1.9% and the Conference Board Labor Differential approaching zero, employers have considerably less reason to bid aggressively for workers. The result is exactly what the chart shows: wage growth continues drifting lower even though layoffs remain historically subdued.

This is an important distinction for the Fed's inflation debate. September Average Hourly Earnings at 3.0% year over year provide little evidence that the current inflation problem is originating from labor. Wage growth has moderated alongside quits, hiring, and worker perceptions of outside opportunities. Combined with the productivity and Unit Labor Cost data discussed previously, the domestic wage mechanism looks considerably more benign than the supply-side inflation pressure visible in Oil, Delivery Times, and ISM Prices Paid.

The income side, however, deserves more attention. Average weekly hours were unchanged at 34.4, leaving Aggregate Weekly Hours flat for the month. Aggregate Payrolls increased only 0.2%, down sharply from August's 0.7% increase. Aggregate labor income remains roughly 4.2% above last year, but the incremental impulse is clearly slowing.

That becomes particularly important when inflation remains elevated. Nominal wage growth of 3.0% provides substantially less protection for households when PCE inflation is running around 3.4% and highly visible necessities such as energy remain under pressure. The problem for consumers is therefore shifting from unemployment toward real purchasing power. Most workers are keeping their jobs, but their wages are no longer accelerating fast enough to comfortably absorb another increase in the cost of living.

This creates a difficult combination for consumption. Low layoffs preserve the income floor, but weak hiring reduces opportunities to increase household income through employment transitions. Depressed quits limit workers' bargaining power, while higher energy and other supply-driven prices consume a larger share of existing wages. The consumer does not need to experience a major employment contraction for discretionary spending to come under pressure if real wage growth remains compressed for long enough.

The report also complicates the Fed's near-term reaction function. The September payroll miss, downward revisions, weaker employment breadth, and softer wages substantially reduce the argument for immediately following September's hike with another increase in October. The employment side of the mandate is no longer providing the same unrestricted runway for tightening that August appeared to provide.

December remains a different question. The weakness in payrolls is increasingly clear, but the inflation pressure discussed above has not disappeared. Oil remains elevated, Delivery Times are lengthening, ISM Prices Paid has surged to 77.9, and the Fed remains concerned about allowing another series of supply shocks to become embedded in expectations. The tension is becoming sharper because the two sides of the mandate are now moving in opposite directions.

That leaves the Fed facing an increasingly uncomfortable configuration: labor demand and wage growth are slowing at the same time supply-driven inflation remains elevated. Higher rates can weaken the former considerably more easily than they can solve the latter.

For now, September argues for patience rather than panic. The labor market is weakening, but layoffs still tell us it is not breaking. The more important development is that the wage and income cushion protecting consumers from higher prices is becoming progressively thinner.

Higher inflation alongside lower wage growth is a considerably more difficult consumer environment than the headline 4.2% Unemployment Rate alone would suggest.

Bottom Line

Policy Is Cooling What It Can Reach

Taken together, this week's data sharpen the tradeoff rather than resolve it. The labor market is cooling through fewer opportunities, weaker mobility, slower payroll growth, and moderating wages rather than through widespread layoffs. Inflation, meanwhile, is increasingly being sustained by areas where higher interest rates offer only an indirect solution. The Fed can suppress demand, but it cannot manufacture energy, power capacity, semiconductors, or the industrial equipment required for the current investment cycle.

Markets are reflecting the same imbalance. Treasury volatility has risen substantially while index volatility remains subdued, and an unusually large share of S&P 500 constituents is behaving independently of the index itself. This is not yet systemic stress. It is fragmentation. As long as credit remains orderly, layoffs remain low, and mega-cap earnings support the index, that fragmentation can persist considerably longer than conventional breadth or valuation signals might suggest.

The risk is that continued tightening eventually connects these currently separate pressure points. A labor market with few outside opportunities becomes more vulnerable if layoffs begin rising. A fragmented equity market becomes more vulnerable if correlations increase. Elevated Treasury volatility becomes more consequential if it migrates into credit. And supply-driven inflation becomes considerably more damaging if the Fed responds by weakening demand faster than supply constraints can normalize.

The constructive path requires relatively little to go right, but it does require the pressure to stop intensifying. Stabilizing yields, easing supply constraints, and continued low layoffs would give wages and real incomes time to recover while allowing the weakness beneath the equity index to repair through rotation rather than liquidation.

For now, the economy is slowing where policy works while inflation remains stubborn where policy works least effectively. That is the tension tying the entire picture together. The system has absorbed higher rates remarkably well so far. The next test is whether policymakers recognize the difference between resilience that provides room for additional tightening and resilience that is gradually being consumed by it.
